title: Your Own Documents and Sources — Module Quiz

items.q: Grounding an answer means:
options: Asking the model to be more careful before answering
Supplying the source passage in the request so the model reads rather than recalls
Restricting the model to shorter answers
items.explain: The task changes from recall to comprehension, and comprehension is what these systems are genuinely good at.

items.q: The most useful property a grounded answer gains is that it:
options: Costs fewer tokens
Can be checked against a source you control
Is guaranteed to be factually correct
items.explain: Grounding usually costs more, not less — passages are tokens. What it buys is a place to look, which is what makes E7's two-minute check possible.

items.q: A retrieved passage mentions the topic but does not contain the answer. A well-built system should:
options: Answer from it anyway, since it was the best match
State that the passage does not answer the question, and stop
Quietly fall back on the model's general knowledge
items.explain: Falling back un-grounds the answer while keeping every appearance of a grounded one, which is worse than never claiming to be checkable.

items.q: Why is a one-sentence passage often a poor unit of retrieval?
options: It uses too few tokens to be worth sending
It frequently cannot be understood alone, so it becomes confident-looking noise
Short passages always score lower in ranking
items.explain: "This does not apply to orders placed before that date" retrieves cleanly and means nothing without its surroundings.

items.q: Splitting a document every 1,000 characters is a weak default because:
options: The passages end up too large for most context windows
The boundary lands arbitrarily — mid-sentence, mid-table, between a heading and its paragraph
It makes embeddings more expensive to compute
items.explain: The length is not the issue; the arbitrariness is. A document's own headings mark where topics genuinely change.

items.q: When you lift a paragraph out from under a heading, you should:
options: Leave it as it is — the document still has the heading
Repeat the heading inside the passage so it keeps its subject
Merge it with the next section to preserve context
items.explain: Retrieval sees only the passage. Context left behind in the document is context the passage does not have.

items.q: The test of a well-cut passage is:
options: It falls within the target character range
Read cold, with nothing around it, you can still tell what it is about
It contains at least one likely search keyword
items.explain: Retrieval sees exactly what you see reading it cold, so anything ambiguous to you will be matched on the wrong questions.

items.q: Keyword matching beats meaning-based search when the question involves:
options: A concept the document describes in different words
An exact string like a product code, error number or clause reference
A long, conversationally phrased request
items.explain: Nobody paraphrases ERR_5521. Meaning-based search may return passages about errors generally, which is precisely not what was asked.

items.q: A user asks "can I send this back?" of a policy that only says "returns". This is handled by:
options: Keyword matching, since the words are simple
Meaning-based matching, since the phrasings sit near each other despite sharing no words
Increasing the number of passages retrieved
items.explain: This is the vocabulary gap embeddings exist to close, and exactly where keyword matching returns nothing at all.

items.q: Why should a word appearing in nearly every passage be weighted down?
options: Common words are usually less meaningful
It cannot discriminate — matching it does not narrow the field at all
It inflates the cost of the retrieval step
items.explain: Retrieval is discrimination. A term shared by everything separates nothing, however meaningful it is in ordinary use.

items.q: On Lrnon's index, "What is the capital of France?" scored higher than any genuine in-scope question. What does that demonstrate?
options: The scoring formula contained a bug
A rare word appearing incidentally can outrank a common word appearing meaningfully
Out-of-scope questions need a keyword blocklist
items.explain: The score was computed correctly, which is what makes it instructive. A second gate on how much of the question is covered catches this class.

items.q: Why is a single relevance score insufficient to decide whether anything relevant was found?
options: Scores vary between models and cannot be compared
A ranked list always has a top item, even when everything in it is irrelevant
Scores are too slow to compute for large collections
items.explain: Ranking answers "which is most relevant", never "is anything relevant at all". Those are different questions and only the second gates a refusal.

items.q: The minimum useful evaluation set for retrieval is:
options: A published benchmark for your document type
Around twenty real questions, each with the passage that should be found written down
One question per document in the collection
items.explain: An hour's work, and enough to tell whether a change improved things or broke them.

items.q: Why write down the expected passage before running the question?
options: It speeds up the evaluation
Judging afterwards whether the result seems good enough will rationalise almost anything
It is needed to compute a recall score
items.explain: Deciding first makes the outcome binary. Deciding after seeing the output is an opinion, and a degraded system keeps passing it.

items.q: An answer is wrong. The first thing to check is:
options: Whether the prompt could be phrased more clearly
Whether the right passage was retrieved at all
Whether a larger model would perform better
items.explain: If the passage never arrived, no prompt or model change can help — and that is where hours disappear, tuning the half that was working.

items.q: Your evaluation questions should mostly come from:
options: Questions you thought of while testing the system
Questions real users actually ask, in their own words
Questions with a single unambiguous keyword match
items.explain: Questions you invent are shaped by knowing what the system can do, which is exactly the bias that conceals its failures.

items.q: Your instructions and the retrieved passages must occupy separate channels because:
options: It reduces the token count of the request
Otherwise text inside a document is structurally indistinguishable from your own instructions
Most APIs reject requests that combine them
items.explain: Documents can be edited, sometimes by strangers. A separate system field is what lets the model see the boundary at all.

items.q: An answer cites [7] but only four passages were supplied. This should be treated as:
options: A valid citation using the model's own numbering
A fabricated citation, equivalent to citing nothing
Evidence a fifth passage was retrieved but not displayed
items.explain: It is the shape of a citation without the substance. A range check is what turns "cites its sources" into a property rather than a hope.

items.q: Supplying ten passages instead of four to compensate for weak ranking is a problem because:
options: There is no problem — more context is always better
You pay for the workaround on every request, and burying the good passage makes it harder to use
Models cannot process more than five passages reliably
items.explain: Volume compensating for ranking is a recurring cost and a precision loss. Fixing the ranking is cheaper on every call thereafter.

items.q: A policy is withdrawn and its file deleted, but its passages remain indexed. The consequence is:
options: Retrieval fails for that topic, which is noticeable
The system keeps answering confidently from retracted guidance, with nothing visible to reveal it
Answers become slower but remain correct
items.explain: The index is what retrieval reads, not the folder — and there is no stale document on screen to notice, only an answer.

items.q: Rebuilding the whole index on a schedule has one underrated advantage over incremental updates:
options: It is faster on large collections
It handles deletion for free, because the new index contains only what currently exists
It produces more accurate embeddings
items.explain: Deletion is the case incremental pipelines forget, precisely because skipping it fails silently.

items.q: Instructing a model to refuse when the passages fall short is:
options: Sufficient on its own with a capable model
Worth doing, but not a guarantee — something after the answer must be able to reject it
Unnecessary once a retrieval threshold exists
items.explain: A prompt is a request; a return statement is not. If refusing is the point of the system, enforce it where it cannot be talked out of.

items.q: What happens to a document's access controls when it is indexed into a shared retrieval system?
options: The index preserves them automatically
They stop applying unless you rebuild them — any asker can reach any passage
They apply to answers but not to retrieval
items.explain: The index has one rule: reachable by anyone who can ask. The salary review in the same folder as the handbook is now answerable to everyone.

items.q: You are unsure whether a document should be indexed. The safer default is:
options: Include it — an unanswered question is worse than an over-broad answer
Leave it out — a gap gets reported, while a leak produces correct-looking answers and no visible failure
Include it with a reduced relevance weight
items.explain: The two errors are not symmetrical. One is self-reporting and recoverable; the other cannot be un-answered afterwards.
